page: Google Cloud Platform c3-standard-176 is a general-purpose compute instance built on the x86_64 architecture. It features 176 dedicated virtual CPUs across 88 physical cores powered by an Intel Xeon 8481C processor operating at 2.7 GHz. The instance is provisioned with 704 GB of system memory, matching a standard 1:4 vCPU-to-RAM ratio with 4.0 GB per vCPU. Cache infrastructure includes 48 KB of L1 data cache, 2 MB of L2 cache, and a shared 105 MB L3 cache. It incorporates hardware acceleration flags including AVX-512, AMX (Advanced Matrix Extensions with tile and INT8 support), and hardware cryptographic suites such as VAES and SHA-NI. The instance contains zero GPUs and provides no bundled local storage, requiring network-attached block storage for persistence.

Benchmark measurements reflect strong multi-threaded computational and throughput capabilities alongside typical single-thread execution rates. In stress-ng, multi-core CPU execution ranks in the top tier at 146,518.46, whereas single-core performance settles in the median range at 1,624.48. High-density instruction capabilities are visible in the PassMark extended instructions score of 176,554.44 and encryption rating of 152,641.42. High-volume data operations benefit from top-tier memory bandwidth, reaching 447.9 GB/sec on uncached read blocks and 197.06 GB/sec on write operations. In-memory data structures perform exceptionally well, logging 165.0 million operations per second in Redis SET evaluations alongside static web throughput reaching 126.15 GB/sec. Large language model prompt processing also demonstrates strong results across various model sizes, aided by AMX matrix support.

The primary tradeoff of the c3-standard-176 lies in its reliance on external storage for persistent disk access, meaning input/output pipelines are bound by network attachment limits rather than local NVMe speeds. Single-threaded metrics, including compression and decompression tasks, show baseline performance, meaning scale must be achieved through parallelism. Resource density provides favorable operational efficiency when consolidating distributed enterprise environments into large, centralized processing tiers. The platform is best fitted for high-concurrency enterprise web serving, large-scale Redis or in-memory caches, matrix and vector processing pipelines, continuous integration compilation clusters, and parallel scientific simulation workloads.
